# Introduction

## Background

Resource conservation and stewardship in Canada is governed through a decentralized, multi-sector array of constitutional authority administered through federal, provincial, territorial, and municipal governments (Ray et al 2021; Campbell and Thomas 2002). Stemming from the Constitution Act, legislative control over ecological conservation has been a reactionary process of assigning authority to multiple jurisdictions over new environmental issues as they arise, which creates a complex and overlapping distribution of governance (Becklumb 2013). This patchwork of authority is most prominent in Pacific salmon management due to the complicated geographic nature of the salmon anadromous life cycle, spanning a variety of freshwater and marine ecosystems coast-wide and across international boundaries.

While legislation and programs may often operate on a sector-by-sector and individual resource basis, integrated stewardship relies on scale-appropriate planning and decision making (Ray et al 2021). The need for collaborative, transparent decision-making in salmon management is recognized throughout policies, plans, and initiatives, such as the Pacific Salmon Strategy Initiative and the Wild Salmon Policy. Successful conservation and rebuilding of Pacific salmon populations therefore requires coordination of activities across regulatory frameworks. However, such coordination requires adequate organizational capacity and systems for effective implementation to ensure that regulatory controls and mitigation activities address underlying threats and factors that limit salmon habitat capacity and reduce population productivity.

## Legislation by anthropogenic threats to salmon

The plural federal and provincial legal systems govern and uphold the human activities that impact Pacific salmon productivity and habitat capacity (Ulaski et al 2025). Acts and regulations in British Columbia might be designed to address one broad category of human activity; however, this activity can cover many aspects of salmon management. For example, the provincial <em>Forest and Range Practices Act</em> is specific to forestry practices and planning, along with cattle ranging practices, but in terms of salmon threats, these activities impact many aspects including stream hydrology, water temperature, effluent, riparian habitat destruction, watercourse changes from road infrastructure, and the spread of invasive species. Figure 1 shows the fractured, yet interconnected, relationships between statutes and responsible minister and agency (Canada: <a href= "https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/tablepublicstatutes/index.html" style="color:#668899">Table of Public Statutes and Responsible Ministers</a>; British Columbia: <a href="https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/content/amr/amr/1662622382/?xsl=/templates/browse.xsl" style="color:#668899">Acts/Ministers' Responsibilities</a>). 

```{r sankey-legislation-to-agency-by-section, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)
library(networkD3)

# 🔌 Connect to the database
db_path <- here("output", "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# 🗂️ Load tables
agencies <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "agencies"))
legislation <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationMetadata"))
paragraphs <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationParagraphs"))
dbDisconnect(conn)

# 🧮 Compute unique section count per legislation_id
section_counts <- paragraphs[!is.na(Section), .(
  section_count = uniqueN(Section)
), by = legislation_id]

# 🔗 Merge with legislation metadata to get act_name and jurisdiction
section_counts <- merge(section_counts, legislation[, .(legislation_id, act_name, legislation_name, jurisdiction)], by = "legislation_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 🔗 Merge with agencies to get agency-act pairs
sankey_data <- merge(agencies, section_counts, by = "act_name", all.x = TRUE)

# 🎨 Define color palette
jurisdiction_colors <- list(
  Federal = "#996666",     # Red
  Provincial = "#668899"   # Blue
)

# 🔁 Function to build Sankey for a given jurisdiction
build_sankey <- function(data, jurisdiction_label, color_map) {
  data <- data[jurisdiction == jurisdiction_label]
  if (nrow(data) == 0) {
    cat(sprintf("<p>No data for %s jurisdiction.</p>", jurisdiction_label))
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  
  nodes <- unique(c(data$act_name, data$agency))
  nodes_dt <- data.table(name = nodes)
  
  # Assign group based on jurisdiction
  nodes_dt[, group := jurisdiction_label]
  
  # Flip direction: legislation ➝ agency
  data[, source := match(act_name, nodes) - 1]
  data[, target := match(agency, nodes) - 1]
  
  links <- data[, .(source, target, value = section_count), by = .(source, target)]
  
  sankeyNetwork(
    Links = links,
    Nodes = nodes_dt,
    Source = "source",
    Target = "target",
    Value = "value",
    NodeID = "name",
    fontSize = 10,
    nodeWidth = 30,
    NodeGroup = "group",
    colourScale = JS(
      "d3.scaleOrdinal()
         .domain(['Federal', 'Provincial'])
         .range(['#996666', '#668899'])"
    )
  )
}

# 🧭 Federal Sankey
cat("<h3>Federal Jurisdiction: Legislation ➝ Agency</h3>")
build_sankey(sankey_data, "Federal", jurisdiction_colors)

# 🧭 Provincial Sankey
cat("<h3>Provincial Jurisdiction: Legislation ➝ Agency</h3>")
build_sankey(sankey_data, "Provincial", jurisdiction_colors)
```

<p style="text-align: left;">
  <em>Figure 1. Federal and provincial acts and regulations by the responsible minister (line thickness by section count).</em>
</p>

## Purpose and objectives

This report outlines a framework and process to relate human activities that threaten Pacific salmon abundance, biology, and ecology to their regulatory statutes. The overall goal of this effort was to better understand the legislative context that governs Pacific salmon in British Columbia related to human activities across jurisdictions. To achieve this, the more specific objectives were to:

<div style="margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px">
<ol>
<li>create a process and tool to categorize specific legislation by anthropogenic threats to Pacific salmon;</li>
<li>assess legislative factors by threat categorization; and</li>
<li>assess threats in a current salmon management context.</li>
</ol>
</div>

⚠️ Disclaimer: none of the information presented in this report qualifies as legal advice. The authors of this report are aquatic biologists with little to no legal training.

To better categorize legislation aligned with salmon threats and create an interface between biological management and the regulatory context, this study defined discrete areas of administrative responsibility for Pacific salmon as “management domains.”

# Methods

## Management domain developement

### International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Threat Categories

Management decisions and activities related to salmon are often in response to identifiable threats to salmon health and population status. Human systems can be categorized as direct threats to biodiversity more specifically for conservation strategies (Salafsky et al 2024). The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Conservation Measures Partnership (CMP) has developed a hierarchical grouping of threats used globally by conservation practitioners. IUCN direct threat categories are widely used to assess threats as part of IUCN red list assessments, as well as, in status assessments for Pacific salmon populations conducted by the Committee for the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC). For this study, the <a href=" https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1yfm7ua9hQJpjycx6FYQJ6Jy5LA4bP0XP61EW3-sX8ZY/edit?gid=179026760#gid=179026760" style="color:#668899">IUCN - CMP Direct Threats Classification 4.0</a> was used to categorize legislation by direct threats to salmon conservation. Level 2 threat classification was used as the finest resolution that could be applied consistently. 

Legislative clauses that influence Pacific salmon governance in British Columbia are not always associated with conservation threats. As well, some clauses may involve all threats. For example, statutes that outline species status or determine ecological reserves have relevance to how salmon are managed, but can’t be attributed to any one IUCN threat category. Pacific salmon life history also ranges over a broad geography of marine and freshwater habitat (including terrestrial watershed aspects), touching on almost every conservation threat available. Management domains were identified through this study as a clearer and more comprehensive alignment between regulatory administrative concern and conservation threat categories (Figure 1).

Management domains represent a reframing of multi-jurisdictional issues by salmon management concern rather than specific agency. This tool can then be used by practitioners to view actual binding legislation when considering actions or proposals. Using the IUCN-CMP Direct Threats Classification 4.0, and other broader categories identified through this exercise process, the following management domains were identified:


## Scope

Regulatory language that can be matched to management domain and IUCN threat categories is not inherently specific to Pacific salmon. However, clauses fall within a relevance spectrum. For example, a clause that states catch limits for Chinook salmon would be much more specific to salmon management than a clause that states that a minister shall include ecological integrity objectives in a park management plan. Both clauses influence salmon governance and management, but one clause is more direct. A “scope” classification was developed as part of this study to parallel management domains and categorize clauses based on their direct application to Pacific salmon. The scope was determined by the specificity of the language used in the section. The scope categories were defined as follows:

<div style="margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px">
<ul style='list-style-type: none'>
<li><strong>1 – Salmon</strong>: refers to Pacific salmon specifically</li>
<li><strong>2 – Fish</strong>: refers to fish that include salmon</li>
<li><strong>3 – Habitat</strong>: refers to any habitat that includes salmon habitat</li>
<li><strong>4 – Governance</strong>: refers to administrative processes and structure</li>
</ul>
</div>

The scope assignment process was linked but occurred independent of the management domain and IUCN threat assignment process. The “1 – Salmon” scope was assigned based solely on salmon keywords (salmon, Chinook, sockeye, etc.), regardless of management domain or IUCN threat. The “2 – Fish” and “3 – Habitat” scopes align directly to IUCN threats (unless already classified as “1 – Salmon”). The “4 – Governance” scope was applied last in a separate matching process.

## Keyword matching process

Assessment of legislative context is prone to subjective interpretation. The inclusion and exclusion of both the overall acts and the clauses within the acts creates points of assumption and bias. For this exercise we cast as wide a net as possible and created a process that is publicly accessible, automated, and repeatable. Other researchers may repeat this process as future legislation and language changes. The process steps are:

<div style="margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px">
<ol>
<li>Legislation accumulation and review (CanLii)</li>
<li>Parse legislation by clause, section, and heading (R)</li>
<li>Match management domain and IUCN threat keywords to clauses (R)</li>
<li>Assign Scope (R)</li>
<li>Match clause type keywords to clauses (R)</li>
</ol>
</div>

### Legislation accumulation and review</strong>

This review focused on established Canadian federal and British Columbian provincial legislation (acts and regulations) for inclusion in the management domain process. Specific departmental policy frameworks and processes were not included throughout this exercise unless specifically referenced in the statutes because these executive strategies are prone to changes in the political, administrative, and budgetary landscape. Indigenous legislation, Yukon Territorial legislation, municipal bylaws, and international conventions were not included explicitly. Although this other legislation is pivotal in the management of Pacific salmon, considering this regionally diverse administration was outside the scope of this legislative review in terms of feasibility and timeline.

The <a href="https://www.canlii.org/" style="color:#668899">Canadian Legal Information Institute website, CanLII</a>, provides an excellent resource for searching federal and provincial legislation by keyword search. CanLii was used as a systematic process to collect relevant legislation in the following steps:

<div style="margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px">
<ol>
<li>query Pacific salmon specific terms (salmon, chinook, sockeye, etc.),</li>
<li>extract other keywords from the salmon-specific legislation (word frequency analysis),</li>
<li>query new keywords and IUCN Threat keywords in CanLII to find adjacent legislation,</li>
<li>filter legislation regionally (excluding provinces other than BC), and</li>
<li>download HTML files for relevant legislation directly from government websites.</li>
</ol>
</div>

Through the CanLII website, the user may look up the keywords queried in each act and regulation chosen. This allows the user to quickly assess the context of the word in the legislation and determine if the section is relevant to Pacific salmon. The full list of legislation reviewed in this process is available in Appendix 1.

### Parsing legislation from HTML files

The decentralized overlapping patchwork of Pacific salmon legislation in Canada creates a dynamic such that each act and regulation may contain a variety of administrative responsibilities, possibly attributed to different agencies. However, each act and regulation is comprised of sections and subsections that contain individual clauses that are more specific to a particular management domain. Typological device structure and definitions were derived from the Government of Canada’s <a href="https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/rp-pr/csj-sjc/legis-redact/legistics/p3p1.html" style="color:#668899">“Legistics Paragraphing”</a> (Department of Justice Canada 2022). For the purpose of this review, we used the individual clause (Figure 3) as the sample unit for assignment into management domains and other attributes.  

```{r legistics-paragraphing, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(here)

# Define image path
image_path <- here("Legistics Paragraphing.png")

# Check if image exists
if (file.exists(image_path)) {
  cat(paste0(
    '<div style="max-width:600px; margin-left:0; padding:10px;">',
    '<img src="', image_path, '" alt="Diagram" style="width:85%; height:auto;">',
    '<p style="font-size:0.9em;"><em>Figure 3. Fisheries Act (federal) examples of paragraph parsing from HTML code.</em></p>',
    '</div>'
  ))
} else {
  cat(paste0("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Image file not found: ", image_path, "</p>"))
}
```

Legislation presented on Canadian and British Columbian government websites, and corresponding HTML code, is structured such that each clause is separated individually as a paragraph element. HTML code for paragraph elements is generally consistent across legislation, but section, subsection, and heading elements are not. As shown in Figure 3, “clause” in this study can also refer to subclauses, but also sections, subsections, and opening words (chapeau or umbrella) when they are stand-alone paragraph elements. HTML files were parsed using R and the "rvest" package to extract the text of each clause, then grouped by section and heading.

Storing the data as a database rather than one large spreadsheet allowed for a more dynamic and versatile system for querying, while streamlining the parsing and collection process.

## Keyword and keyphrase development

The management domain and IUCN threat matching process pivoted around an established list of keywords and phrases relevant to Pacific salmon management. Keywords act as a link between categorization and the legislative clauses. Keywords must be specific enough to match an IUCN threat, yet general enough to appear in the acts and regulations that span many decades of legislative language. The keywords originated from three sources:

<div style="margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px">
<ul>
<li><a href=" https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1yfm7ua9hQJpjycx6FYQJ6Jy5LA4bP0XP61EW3-sX8ZY/edit?gid=179026760#gid=179026760" style="color:#668899">IUCN - CMP Direct Threats Classification 4.0</a> examples and definitions</li>
<li>Word frequency analysis (unigrams, bigrams, and trigrams) of collected legislation</li>
<li>Iterative researcher input and revision</li>
</ul> 
</div>

The keyword and keyphrase development process required an iterative researcher revision step because of the varied context of language. While the words used in the IUCN threat definitions may be specific to those threats, they may not be relevant to salmon management and may also have multiple meanings leading to an over-assignment of categories. For example, the word “landfill” is listed on the IUCN threat examples for “1.2 Commercial & Industrial Areas.” Much of the collected legislation deals with pollution, in which landfills are mentioned. However, for salmon habitat, the threat would come from water effluent, and pollution would be a more accurate designation. “Landfill” as a keyword adds many clauses that could be considered outside of the scope of this tool, and so “landfill” was removed from the keyword list.	

Conversely, the word “riparian” is very relevant to salmon habitat management in British Columbia, yet that word doesn’t appear in the IUCN threat examples. As well, “riparian” doesn’t appear in word frequency analyses of other legislation. “Riparian” was added as a keyword solely from the researchers’ discretion.

Researcher subjectivity can influence the process on two fronts:
<div style="margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px">
<ul>
<li>Legislation collection</li>
<li>Keyword and keyphrase list development</li>
</ul> 
</div>

However, using keyword lists allows for the subjectivity to be acknowledged, and the keyword lists to be reported such that the process may be repeatable. The keyword list is shown in Appendix II. 

### Multiple matches

Management domains can overlap within sections and clauses. For example the provincial Land-based Finfish Waste Control Regulation (Environmental Management Act) states in Section 2 that: “The owner of a land-based finfish facility is exempt from section 6 (2) and (3) of the Environmental Management Act with respect to the discharge of wastes from the land-based finfish facility if the owner…” This clause matched appropriately with both the “Aquaculture and Hatcheries” and “Pollution” management domains. Because the matching process allows for multiple keywords to be matched per clause, this method allows for an assessment of co-occurrences and connections between management domains.

## Legislative context (clause types)

The process of parsing legislation by clause and section, then matching categories by keywords also allows for other possible categorizations. Similar to management domains and IUCN threats, the nature of the clauses was also matched in terms of the “clause type.” Clauses, in general, fit into groupings by their context and the nature of their intent. For this exercise, the categories and keywords were developed solely by the researchers through a subjective process; however, the keywords are listed in Appendix III allowing for the work to be transparent and repeatable.

```{r clause-type-list, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)

# Define database path and confirm it exists
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  # Connect to the database
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # Retrieve unique Clause Type label_values
  query <- "
    SELECT DISTINCT label_value
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'Clause Type' AND label_value IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY label_value
  "
  clause_values <- dbGetQuery(conn, query)$label_value
  
  # Disconnect from the database
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # Output as indented unordered HTML list
  if (length(clause_values) > 0) {
    cat("<div style='margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px;'>\n")
    cat("  <h4>Clause Type Categories:</h4>\n")
    cat("  <ul>\n")
    for (val in clause_values) {
      cat(paste0("    <li>", val, "</li>\n"))
    }
    cat("  </ul>\n")
    cat("</div>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No Clause Type values found in the database.</p>\n")
  }
}


```

## Current salmon management

The Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC) assesses the current status of aquatic species, including Pacific salmon stocks, as part of the Species at Risk Act (SARA) process (Arbeider et al 2020). Salmon populations are grouped into genetically and ecologically distinct Diagnostic Units (DU) for the purpose of assessment. When a DU is classified as Threatened, Endangered or Extirpated, a Recovery Potential Assessment (RPA) process is initiated, which calculates risk incorporating the same IUCN-CMP threat classification used in this legislative assessment.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada published “Canada’s Policy for Conservation of Wild Pacific Salmon,” or the Wild Salmon Policy (WSP), in 2005, which outlines managing salmon in Conservation Units (CU), differing somewhat from the DUs used by COSEWIC. Conservation Units are defined in the WSP as: “a group of wild salmon sufficiently isolated from other groups that, if extirpated is very unlikely to recolonize naturally within an acceptable timeframe, such as a human lifetime or a specified number of salmon generations” (Canada ed. 2005). Since CUs are the most current unit for managing salmon in British Columbia, we incorporated CUs in this effort.

The following Conservation Units were included in this assessment: 

```{r cu-species-cu-name-html-list, results='asis', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)

# Connect to the database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# Query and filter the data
cu_data <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "cu_ranking"))
filtered_cu <- cu_data[!is.na(rpa_threat_ranking) & rpa_threat_ranking != "", .(cu_species, cu_name)]
unique_cu <- unique(filtered_cu)

# Render as HTML unordered list
cat("<ul>\n")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(unique_cu))) {
  item <- paste0(unique_cu$cu_species[i], " | ", unique_cu$cu_name[i])
  cat(paste0("  <li>", item, "</li>\n"))
}
cat("</ul>\n")

# Disconnect
dbDisconnect(conn)
```

# Results

## Management domains and IUCN threat categories

Management domains were identified within all the collected statutes. Pollution was the management domain with the highest section count (Figure 4), split almost evenly between federal and provincial jurisdictions. Human Disturbance (research activities) and Climate Change and Natural Disasters had the fewest section count. Fisheries was in the top three for section count, with a majority of sections under federal jurisdiction. Water Use and Watercourse Modifications was in the top four for section count, with a majority of sections under provincial jurisdiction. This count indicates an underlying possibly dysfunctional relationship where salmon harvest is controlled federally while habitat aspects are governed provincially.

```{r management-domain-tally, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)

db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # ✅ Step 1: Get Management Domain-labeled paragraphs directly from label_value
  domain_labels <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, label_value AS management_domain
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'Management Domain' AND label_value IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  # 📄 Step 2: Load paragraph metadata
  paragraph_meta <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, Section, legislation_id
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
    WHERE Section IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🔗 Step 3: Merge with metadata
  merged <- merge(domain_labels, paragraph_meta, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  
  # 📊 Step 4: Tally by management_domain
  domain_tally <- merged[, .(
    clauses = uniqueN(paragraph_id),
    sections = uniqueN(paste(legislation_id, Section, sep = "_")),
    statutes = uniqueN(legislation_id)
  ), by = management_domain][order(management_domain)]
  
  # 📦 Totals
  total_clauses <- sum(domain_tally$clauses)
  total_sections <- sum(domain_tally$sections)
  total_statutes <- uniqueN(merged$legislation_id)
  
  # 🖥️ Output
  if (nrow(domain_tally) > 0) {
    cat("<ul style='list-style-type: none; padding-left: 0; margin: 0;'>\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(domain_tally))) {
      cat(sprintf("<li><strong>%s:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections | %d clauses</li>\n",
                  domain_tally$management_domain[i],
                  domain_tally$statutes[i],
                  domain_tally$sections[i],
                  domain_tally$clauses[i]))
    }
    cat(sprintf("<li style='margin-top: 10px;'><strong>Total:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections | %d clauses</li>\n",
                total_statutes, total_sections, total_clauses))
    cat("</ul>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No Management Domain labels found.</p>\n")
  }
}


```

```{r section-count-by-management-domain, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis', fig.width=12, fig.height=9}
# 📦 Load required libraries
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)

# 📁 Define path to the SQLite database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  # 🔌 Connect to the database
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # 🗂️ Load paragraph labels filtered by Management Domain
  paragraph_labels <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, label_value AS management_domain
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'Management Domain' AND label_value IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  # 🗂️ Load paragraph and legislation metadata including Section
  paragraph_table <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, legislation_id, Section
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
  "))
  
  legislation_metadata <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT legislation_id, jurisdiction
    FROM LegislationMetadata
  "))
  
  # 🔌 Disconnect from the database
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🔗 Join labels with paragraph and legislation metadata
  domain_data <- merge(paragraph_labels, paragraph_table, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  domain_data <- merge(domain_data, legislation_metadata, by = "legislation_id", all.x = TRUE)
  
  # 🧼 Normalize management domain labels
  domain_data[, management_domain := str_squish(management_domain)]
  
  # 📊 Summarize counts by unique Section-legislation_id pairs
  domain_counts <- domain_data[!is.na(Section), .(
    section_Count = uniqueN(paste(Section, legislation_id))
  ), by = .(management_domain, jurisdiction)]
  
  # 🧮 Order management domains by total section count (largest to smallest)
  domain_order <- domain_counts[, .(total = sum(section_Count)), by = management_domain][order(-total)]
  domain_counts[, management_domain := factor(management_domain, levels = rev(domain_order$management_domain))]  # reverse for top-down
  
  # 🎨 Create stacked horizontal bar chart
  ggplot(domain_counts, aes(
    x = management_domain,
    y = section_Count,
    fill = jurisdiction
  )) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 0.8) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c("Federal" = "#996666", "Provincial" = "#668899", "Unknown" = "#999999"),
      guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "Section Count by Management Domain",
      x = "Management Domain",
      y = "Unique Section Count",
      fill = "Jurisdiction"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
    )
}


```

<p style="text-align: left;">
  <em>Figure 4. Count of sections matched by management domains stacked by jurisdiction.</em>
</p>

IUCN Level 2 categories are more specific, and the categorization process matched to 25 categories (Figure 5) that parallel the management domain categories. Multiple IUCN threats comprise a management domain; however Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution (9.1) matched with the highest number of sections (as in the management domains) followed by Fishing, Harvesting & Controlling Aquatic Species (5.4). Eight IUCN threat categories make up the Water Use and Watercourse Modifications management domain, but Dams & Water Management / Use (7.2) has the majority of matches.

## Scope

Scope categories were assigned to clauses and sections parallel to management domains and IUCN threat categories. Language specific to Pacific salmon management was found in far fewer sections than indirect, less specific language (Figure 6). Only 74 sections in 22 statutes mention Pacific salmon, while 2,607 sections in 165 statutes mention habitat aspects that impact salmon. It is also interesting to note that the federal Fisheries Act does not use the word "salmon" or any salmon-specific keywords (1 - Salmon) at all, only the regulations made under the Fisheries Act use salmon-specific language.

```{r scope-tally, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)

db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # ✅ Step 1: Get scope-labeled paragraphs from Management Domain and Salmon Scope
  scope_labels <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, scope
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type IN ('Management Domain', 'Salmon Scope') AND scope IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  # 📄 Step 2: Load paragraph metadata
  paragraph_meta <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, Section, legislation_id
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
    WHERE Section IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🔗 Step 3: Merge with metadata
  merged <- merge(scope_labels, paragraph_meta, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  
  # 📊 Step 4: Tally by scope
  scope_tally <- merged[, .(
    clauses = uniqueN(paragraph_id),
    sections = uniqueN(paste(legislation_id, Section, sep = "_")),
    statutes = uniqueN(legislation_id)
  ), by = scope][order(scope)]
  
  # 📦 Totals
  total_clauses <- sum(scope_tally$clauses)
  total_sections <- sum(scope_tally$sections)
  total_statutes <- uniqueN(merged$legislation_id)
  
  # 🖥️ Output
  if (nrow(scope_tally) > 0) {
    cat("<ul style='list-style-type: none; padding-left: 0; margin: 0;'>\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(scope_tally))) {
      cat(sprintf("<li><strong>%s:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections |  %d clauses</li>\n",
                  scope_tally$scope[i],
                  scope_tally$statutes[i],
                  scope_tally$sections[i],
                  scope_tally$clauses[i]))
    }
    cat(sprintf("<li style='margin-top: 10px;'><strong>Total:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections | %d clauses</li>\n",
                total_statutes, total_sections, total_clauses))
    cat("</ul>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No scope labels found for Management Domain or Salmon Scope.</p>\n")
  }
}
```

```{r ggplot-multiscope-donut-final, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggforce)

# Connect to the database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# Load tables
paragraph_label_table <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "paragraph_label_table"))
paragraph_table <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationParagraphs"))
dbDisconnect(conn)

# Get paragraph_ids tagged with Salmon Scope
salmon_scope_ids <- paragraph_label_table[
  label_type == "Salmon Scope" & scope == "1 - Salmon", paragraph_id
]

# Get Management Domain labels linked to those Salmon Scope paragraphs
salmon_ring <- paragraph_label_table[
  label_type == "Management Domain" & paragraph_id %in% salmon_scope_ids
][, scope := "1 - Salmon"]

# Get other Management Domain entries (non-Salmon scopes)
other_rings <- paragraph_label_table[
  label_type == "Management Domain" & !(paragraph_id %in% salmon_scope_ids)
]

# Combine all scope-tagged Management Domain entries
md_labels <- rbind(salmon_ring, other_rings)

# Merge with paragraph_table to get legislation_id and Section
merged_data <- merge(
  md_labels,
  paragraph_table[, .(paragraph_id, legislation_id, Section)],
  by = "paragraph_id",
  all.x = TRUE
)

# Count unique Sections per legislation_id, grouped by scope and label_value
raw_counts <- merged_data[
  , .(SectionCount = uniqueN(Section)), by = .(scope, label_value)
]

# Ensure all scope × label_value combinations are represented
all_combos <- CJ(scope = unique(md_labels$scope),
                 label_value = unique(md_labels$label_value))
donut_data <- merge(all_combos, raw_counts, by = c("scope", "label_value"), all.x = TRUE)
donut_data[is.na(SectionCount), SectionCount := 0]

# Assign fixed ring positions for each scope
scope_levels <- sort(unique(donut_data$scope))
scope_radii <- data.table(
  scope = scope_levels,
  r0 = seq(0.3, by = 0.3, length.out = length(scope_levels)),
  r = seq(0.5, by = 0.3, length.out = length(scope_levels)),
  label_radius = seq(0.4, by = 0.3, length.out = length(scope_levels))
)
donut_data <- merge(donut_data, scope_radii, by = "scope")

# Compute arc positions
donut_data <- donut_data %>%
  group_by(scope) %>%
  arrange(label_value) %>%
  mutate(
    total = sum(SectionCount),
    fraction = ifelse(total > 0, SectionCount / total, 0),
    ymax = cumsum(fraction),
    ymin = lag(ymax, default = 0)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Create scope labels
scope_labels <- scope_radii %>%
  mutate(
    x = label_radius * cos(pi / 2),
    y = label_radius * sin(pi / 2)
  )

# Define custom colors for label_value slices
domain_colors <- c(
  "Agriculture" = "greenyellow",
  "Aquaculture and Hatcheries" = "violetred2",
  "Climate Change and Natural Disasters" = "tomato2",
  "Fisheries" = "turquoise2",
  "Forest and Range" = "sienna3",
  "Human Disturbance" = "grey50",
  "Restoration" = "springgreen4",
  "Invasive or Problematic Species and Disease" = "darkorchid3",
  "Mining and Energy" = "grey30",
  "Pollution" = "black",
  "Spatial Designation" = "grey90",
  "Species Status and Assessment" = "grey80",
  "Transportation Infrastructure" = "yellow3",
  "Water Use and Watercourse Modifications" = "skyblue3"
)

# Plot multi-ring donut chart
ggplot(donut_data) +
  geom_arc_bar(aes(
    x0 = 0, y0 = 0,
    r0 = r0, r = r,
    start = 2 * pi * ymin,
    end = 2 * pi * ymax,
    fill = label_value
  ), color = "white") +
  geom_text(data = scope_labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = scope), size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = domain_colors, na.value = "#999999") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = "Management Domain")) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Management Domains Across Scope",
    subtitle = "Each ring represents Scope; slices show Management Domain weight by Section count"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

<p style="text-align: left;"><em>Figure 6. Count of sections as a proportion by management domain categories and tiered by scope.</em></p>

More federal legislation sections matched with salmon harvest categories than provincial, as shown in Figures 4 and 5 above. Pacific salmon-specific language (1 - Salmon scope) also matched more federal statutes, specifically, the British Columbia Sport Fishing Regulations, 1996; National Parks of Canada Fishing Regulations; and Pacific Fishery Regulations 1993 (Figure 7).

## Clause type

Independent of management domain and IUCN threat categories, the clause types (contextual nature of clauses) was assessed by matching "clause type keywords" (Appendix III) to clauses. Authorization & Mandate; Instruction; and Licence, Permitting, & Exemptions matched the largest number of sections, while Prohibition, Restriction, or Limitation matched the fewest. Naturally, the management domains with the highest number of matched sections also had the highest number of matched clause types; however, the density of the clause type matching can be shown relatively (Figure 8).

```{r clause-type-with-domain-tally, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)

db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # ✅ Step 1: Get all labels for paragraphs
  label_data <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, label_type, label_value
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_value IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  # ✅ Step 2: Identify paragraph_ids that have a Management Domain label
  domain_paragraphs <- unique(label_data[label_type == 'Management Domain', paragraph_id])
  
  # ✅ Step 3: Filter Clause Type labels to only those paragraph_ids
  clause_labels <- label_data[
    label_type == 'Clause Type' & paragraph_id %in% domain_paragraphs,
    .(paragraph_id, clause_type = label_value)
  ]
  
  # 📄 Step 4: Load paragraph metadata
  paragraph_meta <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, Section, legislation_id
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
    WHERE Section IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🔗 Step 5: Merge with metadata
  merged <- merge(clause_labels, paragraph_meta, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  
  # 📊 Step 6: Tally by clause_type
  clause_tally <- merged[, .(
    clauses = uniqueN(paragraph_id),
    sections = uniqueN(paste(legislation_id, Section, sep = "_")),
    statutes = uniqueN(legislation_id)
  ), by = clause_type][order(clause_type)]
  
  # 📦 Totals
  total_clauses <- sum(clause_tally$clauses)
  total_sections <- sum(clause_tally$sections)
  total_statutes <- uniqueN(merged$legislation_id)
  
  # 🖥️ Output
  if (nrow(clause_tally) > 0) {
    cat("<ul style='list-style-type: none; padding-left: 0; margin: 0;'>\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(clause_tally))) {
      cat(sprintf("<li><strong>%s:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections | %d clauses </li>\n",
                  clause_tally$clause_type[i],
                  clause_tally$statutes[i],
                  clause_tally$sections[i],
                  clause_tally$clauses[i]))
    }
    cat(sprintf("<li style='margin-top: 10px;'><strong>Total:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections | %d clauses</li>\n",
                total_statutes, total_sections, total_clauses))
    cat("</ul>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No Clause Type labels found in paragraphs with Management Domain labels.</p>\n")
  }
}
```

```{r plot-clause-type-heatmap, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=9}
# 📦 Load required libraries
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)

# 🔌 Connect to the database
db_path <- here("output", "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# 🗂️ Load tables
paragraph_labels       <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "paragraph_label_table"))
legislation_paragraphs <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationParagraphs"))
legislation_metadata   <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationMetadata"))

# 🔌 Disconnect from the database
dbDisconnect(conn)

# 🎯 Extract Clause Type and Management Domain labels
clause_labels <- paragraph_labels[label_type == "Clause Type", .(paragraph_id, clause_type = label_value)]
domain_labels <- paragraph_labels[label_type == "Management Domain", .(paragraph_id, management_domain = label_value)]

# 🔗 Merge clause and domain labels
labeled_paragraphs <- merge(clause_labels, domain_labels, by = "paragraph_id")

# 🔗 Add jurisdiction and section context
paragraph_context <- merge(
  legislation_paragraphs[, .(paragraph_id, legislation_id, Section)],
  legislation_metadata[, .(legislation_id, jurisdiction)],
  by = "legislation_id",
  all.x = TRUE
)
labeled_paragraphs <- merge(labeled_paragraphs, paragraph_context, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 📊 Aggregate counts by unique Section-legislation_id combinations
heatmap_data <- labeled_paragraphs[
  !is.na(clause_type) & !is.na(management_domain) & !is.na(Section),
  .(section_count = uniqueN(paste(Section, legislation_id))),
  by = .(clause_type, management_domain)
]

# 🎨 Plot heat map
ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = clause_type, y = management_domain, fill = section_count)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey87", high = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Clause Type vs. Management Domain",
    x = "Clause Type",
    y = "Management Domain",
    fill = "Section Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14 * font_scale) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 40, b = 20, l = 20),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

## Conservation Units (CUs) and Recovery Potential Assessments (RPAs)

Twenty-seven Conservation Units (CU) were included in this exercise, having been assessed through the COSEWIC Recovery Potential Assessment (RPA) process. RPAs used the same IUCN threat categories for assessment ranked from low to extreme by CU. Figure 9 shows the aggregate of the rankings regardless of threat, but stacked by species. More CUs had IUCN threats ranked from negligible to low while a few CUs had extreme to high rankings, specifically for Chinook and lake type sockeye.

```{r cu-index-tally, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Load libraries
library(here)
library(data.table)
library(RSQLite)
library(ggplot2)

# Connect to SQLite database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# Read cu_ranking table
cu_ranking <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "cu_ranking"))

# Disconnect
dbDisconnect(conn)

# Filter out NA or empty values
cu_ranking <- cu_ranking[
  !is.na(cu_index) & cu_index != "" &
  !is.na(cu_species) & cu_species != "" &
  !is.na(rpa_threat_ranking) & rpa_threat_ranking != "" &
  !is.na(ranking_id)
]

# Convert ranking_id to numeric (if needed)
cu_ranking[, ranking_id := as.numeric(ranking_id)]

# Order rpa_threat_ranking by ranking_id
ordered_levels <- cu_ranking[order(ranking_id), unique(rpa_threat_ranking)]
cu_ranking[, rpa_threat_ranking := factor(rpa_threat_ranking, levels = ordered_levels)]

# Tally unique cu_index values per rpa_threat_ranking and cu_species
cu_tally <- cu_ranking[, .(unique_cu_count = uniqueN(cu_index)), by = .(rpa_threat_ranking, cu_species)]

# Define custom colors for each CU species
custom_colors <- c(
  "Chinook" = "grey",
  "Coho"    = "#9acce4",
  "Sockeye (Lake Type)" = "#996666",
  "Sockeye (River Type)" = "#EBA0A0"
)

# Plot stacked bar chart with custom colors
ggplot(cu_tally, aes(x = rpa_threat_ranking, y = unique_cu_count, fill = cu_species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "CU Count per RPA Threat Ranking",
    x = "RPA Threat Ranking",
    y = "Conservation Unit Count",
    fill = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

<p style="text-align: left;"><em>Figure 9. Conservation Unit (CU) count by IUCN threat ranking through the COSEWIC Recovery Potential Analysis (RPA) process.</em></p>

The RPA process identified two IUCN threat categories as being extreme or extreme-high ranking. Geological Events (10.1) received an extreme ranking, and Dams & Water Management / Use (7.2) received an extreme-high ranking (Figure 10). Appendices IV and V of this report use these categories as case studies to demonstrate how the use of the LAPSE tool framework can identify relevant legislation.


# Discussion

## Domain co-occurence

Show a graphic of domain co-occurrence

```{r management-domain-upset-clean, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(ComplexUpset)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

# Connect to SQLite
db_path <- file.path(here::here("output"), "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# Query Management Domain labels joined with Sections
query <- "
SELECT lp.Section, pl.label_value AS ManagementDomain
FROM paragraph_label_table pl
JOIN LegislationParagraphs lp ON pl.paragraph_id = lp.paragraph_id
WHERE pl.label_type = 'Management Domain' AND lp.Section IS NOT NULL
"
md_data <- as.data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, query))
dbDisconnect(conn)

# Create binary matrix: rows = Sections, columns = Management Domains
md_matrix <- dcast(
  md_data, 
  Section ~ ManagementDomain, 
  fun.aggregate = function(x) as.integer(length(x) > 0), 
  value.var = "ManagementDomain"
)

# Remove Section column to collapse by domain combination only
domain_cols <- setdiff(names(md_matrix), "Section")
md_collapsed <- md_matrix[, ..domain_cols][, .N, by = domain_cols]

# Expand rows by frequency
md_expanded <- md_collapsed[rep(seq_len(.N), times = md_collapsed$N)]
md_expanded$N <- NULL

# Convert to data.frame for ComplexUpset
md_df <- as.data.frame(md_expanded)

# Plot using ComplexUpset
ComplexUpset::upset(
  md_df,
  intersect = domain_cols,
  name = "Management Domain Overlap",
 base_annotations = list(
  'Intersection size' = intersection_size(text = list(size = 0))
),
set_sizes = FALSE
)
```

<br>

```{r plot-domain-cooccurrence-heatmap, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# 📦 Load required libraries
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)

# 🔌 Connect to the database
db_path <- here("output", "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# 🗂️ Load tables
paragraph_labels       <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "paragraph_label_table"))
legislation_paragraphs <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationParagraphs"))
legislation_metadata   <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationMetadata"))
dbDisconnect(conn)

# 🎯 Filter for all Management Domain labels
domain_labels <- paragraph_labels[
  label_type == "Management Domain",
  .(paragraph_id, management_domain = label_value)
]

# 🧭 Add Section and legislation_id context
paragraph_context <- legislation_paragraphs[, .(paragraph_id, legislation_id, Section)]
domain_labels <- merge(domain_labels, paragraph_context, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 🔁 Create pairwise combinations of domains within each Section-legislation_id
domain_pairs <- domain_labels[
  !is.na(management_domain) & !is.na(Section),
  .(domain_list = list(unique(management_domain))),
  by = .(Section, legislation_id)
][lengths(domain_list) > 1]  # Only keep rows with 2+ domains

# 🧮 Generate domain pairs safely
pairwise_data <- domain_pairs[, .(
  domain_x = unlist(lapply(domain_list, function(x) combn(x, 2, simplify = TRUE)[1, ])),
  domain_y = unlist(lapply(domain_list, function(x) combn(x, 2, simplify = TRUE)[2, ]))
)]

# 📊 Count co-occurrences
heatmap_data <- pairwise_data[, .N, by = .(domain_x, domain_y)]

# 🔁 Add reverse pairs for symmetry
reverse_pairs <- heatmap_data[, .(domain_x = domain_y, domain_y = domain_x, N)]
heatmap_data <- rbind(heatmap_data, reverse_pairs)

# 🎨 Plot symmetric heatmap with small count labels and no gridlines
ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = domain_x, y = domain_y, fill = N)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey90", high = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Co-occurrence of Management Domains by Section",
    x = "",
    y = "",
    fill = "Co-occurrence Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 40, b = 20, l = 20),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )



```

```{r top-domain-pairs-display, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)

db_path <- file.path(here("output", "legislation.db"))
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # Load Management Domain labels
  domain_labels <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, label_value AS domain
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'Management Domain' AND label_value IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  # Load paragraph metadata
  paragraph_meta <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, Section, legislation_id
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
    WHERE Section IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # Merge and group by Section-legislation
  merged <- merge(domain_labels, paragraph_meta, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  grouped <- merged[, .(domains = unique(domain)), by = .(Section, legislation_id)]
  
  # Generate domain pairs
  pairwise <- grouped[, {
    if (length(domains) >= 2) {
      combs <- combn(domains, 2, simplify = FALSE)
      # Canonicalize each pair: sort alphabetically
      data.table(
        domain1 = sapply(combs, function(x) sort(x)[1]),
        domain2 = sapply(combs, function(x) sort(x)[2])
      )
    } else {
      NULL
    }
  }, by = .(Section, legislation_id)]
  
  # Count unique co-occurrences
  pair_counts <- pairwise[, .N, by = .(domain1, domain2)]
  
  # Filter and sort
  top_pairs <- pair_counts[N > 75][order(-N)]
  
  # Display formatted output
  if (nrow(top_pairs) > 0) {
    cat("<div style='margin-left: 30px; padding-left: 10px;'>\n")
    cat("  <h4>Top Domain Co-occurrences:</h4>\n")
    cat("  <ul style='list-style-type: none; padding-left: 0;'>\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(top_pairs))) {
      cat(sprintf("    <li><strong>%s</strong> → <strong>%s</strong> – %d sections</li>\n",
                  top_pairs$domain1[i],
                  top_pairs$domain2[i],
                  top_pairs$N[i]))
    }
    cat("  </ul>\n")
    cat("</div>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No domain pairs with more than 75 co-occurrences found.</p>\n")
  }
}
```

## Clause count as a function of keyword quantity

One criticism could be that the more keywords a category has, the more clauses will be labelled. This is likely true. Here’s a scatterplot that shows number of keywords vs the clause count for that category.

```{r iucn-scatterplot-section-count, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=9}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)

# Connect to the database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

# Load label table and keyword table
label_table <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "paragraph_label_table"))
paragraph_table <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationParagraphs"))
iucn_keywords <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "iucn_l2_keywords"))
dbDisconnect(conn)

# Filter for IUCN labels
iucn_labels <- label_table[label_type == "IUCN" & !is.na(label_value)]

# Merge with paragraph table to get Section and legislation_id
iucn_data <- merge(iucn_labels, paragraph_table[, .(paragraph_id, Section, legislation_id)], by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
iucn_data <- iucn_data[!is.na(Section)]

# Aggregate by unique Section-legislation_id combinations
iucn_summary <- iucn_data[, .(
  section_count = uniqueN(paste(Section, legislation_id))
), by = label_value]

# Add keyword count from iucn_l2_keywords
keyword_counts <- iucn_keywords[, .N, by = iucn_l2]
setnames(keyword_counts, "N", "keyword_count")

# Merge both summaries
plot_data <- merge(iucn_summary, keyword_counts, by.x = "label_value", by.y = "iucn_l2", all.x = TRUE)

# Plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = keyword_count, y = section_count, label = label_value)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2c3e50", size = 3) +
  geom_text(hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "IUCN Level 2: Keyword Count vs Section Count",
    x = "Keyword Count (from iucn_l2_keywords)",
    y = "Unique Section Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlim(0, max(plot_data$keyword_count, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.2)

```

```{r act-legislation-summary-table, results='asis', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# 📦 Load required libraries
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)
library(here)
library(reactable)
library(htmltools)

# 🗂️ Step 1: Resolve database path safely
db_path <- here::here("output", "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) stop("Database not found at: ", db_path)

# 🔌 Step 2: Connect and load tables
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)

legislation_paragraphs <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationParagraphs"))
legislation_metadata   <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "LegislationMetadata"))
paragraph_labels       <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "paragraph_label_table"))
clause_type_keywords   <- as.data.table(dbReadTable(conn, "clause_type_keywords"))

dbDisconnect(conn)

# 🧩 Step 3: Extract and collapse labels
clause_labels <- paragraph_labels[label_type == "Clause Type", .(paragraph_id, keyword)]
clause_labels <- merge(clause_labels, clause_type_keywords[, .(keyword, clause_type)], by = "keyword", all.x = TRUE)
clause_labels <- clause_labels[
  , .(clause_type = unique(clause_type)[1]),  # Select only one unique clause type per paragraph
  by = paragraph_id
]

domain_labels <- paragraph_labels[label_type == "Management Domain", .(paragraph_id, management_domain = label_value)]
domain_labels <- domain_labels[, .(management_domain = paste(unique(management_domain), collapse = ", ")), by = paragraph_id]

iucn_labels <- paragraph_labels[label_type == "IUCN", .(paragraph_id, iucn_l2 = label_value)]
iucn_labels <- iucn_labels[, .(iucn_l2 = paste(unique(iucn_l2), collapse = ", ")), by = paragraph_id]

scope_labels <- paragraph_labels[label_type %in% c("Management Domain", "Salmon Scope"), .(paragraph_id, scope)]
scope_labels <- scope_labels[, .(scope = paste(unique(scope), collapse = ", ")), by = paragraph_id]

# 🔗 Step 4: Merge all labels
label_data <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = "paragraph_id", all = TRUE, allow.cartesian = TRUE),
                     list(clause_labels, domain_labels, iucn_labels, scope_labels))

# 🔗 Step 5: Merge with paragraph and metadata
section_data <- merge(
  legislation_paragraphs[, .(paragraph_id, legislation_id, Heading, Section, Paragraph)],
  legislation_metadata[, .(legislation_id, legislation_name, act_name, jurisdiction, legislation_type)],
  by = "legislation_id",
  all.x = TRUE
)

section_data <- merge(section_data, label_data, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 🧠 Step 6: Create combined columns
section_data[, Section_num := as.numeric(Section)]  # Create numeric version for sorting
section_data[, Act := paste(act_name, jurisdiction, sep = " | ")]
section_data[, Legislation := paste(legislation_type, legislation_name, sep = " | ")]
section_data[, HeadingSection := paste(Heading, paste0("Section ", Section), sep = " | ")]

# 📊 Step 7: Aggregate by Act + Legislation + HeadingSection
section_summary <- section_data[
  !is.na(Section),
  .(
    Section_num = unique(Section_num),  # Include numeric section for sorting
    DomainFilter = paste(unique(na.omit(management_domain)), collapse = ", "),
    Paragraphs = paste(unique(na.omit(Paragraph)), collapse = "<br><br>"),
    ManagementDomain = paste(unique(na.omit(management_domain)), collapse = ", "),
    IUCNThreat = paste(unique(na.omit(iucn_l2)), collapse = ", "),
    ClauseType = paste(unique(na.omit(clause_type)), collapse = ", "),
    Scope = paste(unique(na.omit(scope)), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  by = .(Act, Legislation, HeadingSection)
]

# 🧠 Step 8: Format Paragraphs with metadata block
section_summary[, Paragraphs := paste(
  Paragraphs,
  "<br><br>",
  "<div style='font-size: 0.85em; color: #333; background-color: #f9f9f9; padding: 8px; border-left: 4px solid #0074D9;'>",
  sprintf(
    "<span style='color:#0074D9; font-weight:bold;'>Management Domain:</span> %s; <span style='color:#0074D9; font-weight:bold;'>IUCN Threat:</span> %s; <span style='color:#0074D9; font-weight:bold;'>Clause Type:</span> %s; <span style='color:#0074D9; font-weight:bold;'>Scope:</span> %s",
    htmlEscape(ManagementDomain),
    htmlEscape(IUCNThreat),
    htmlEscape(ClauseType),
    htmlEscape(Scope)
  ),
  "</div>",
  sep = ""
)]

# ✅ Sort section_summary by Act (which includes act_name)
section_summary <- section_summary[order(Act, Legislation, Section_num)]

# 🖥️ Step 9: Render reactable inside a responsive container
htmltools::div(
  style = "width: 100%; overflow-x: auto;",
  reactable(
    section_summary[, .(Act, Legislation, HeadingSection, DomainFilter, Paragraphs)],
    elementId = "act-legislation-summary-table",
    groupBy = c("Act", "Legislation"),
    searchable = TRUE,
    pagination = TRUE,
    striped = TRUE,
    bordered = TRUE,
    resizable = TRUE,
    defaultPageSize = 10,
    defaultColDef = colDef(filterable = TRUE),
    columns = list(
      Act = colDef(name = "Act", filterable = TRUE, minWidth = 150),
      Legislation = colDef(name = "Legislation", filterable = TRUE, minWidth = 200),
      HeadingSection = colDef(name = "Heading & Section", filterable = TRUE, minWidth = 150),
      DomainFilter = colDef(name = "Management Domain", filterable = TRUE, show = FALSE),
      Paragraphs = colDef(
        name = "Paragraphs",
        html = TRUE,
        minWidth = 400,
        style = list(fontSize = "0.85em", whiteSpace = "normal")
      )
    )
  )
)
```

## Appendix IV - Case Study: IUCN 10.1 Geological Events

One IUCN threat was assessed as "Extreme" through COSEWIC Recovery Potential Assessment processes, which was the "10.1 Geological Events" threat (DFO 2020; DFO 2022). This threat was assigned to one sockeye and three Chinook conservation units, all in the Fraser Interior area related to the "ongoing effects from Big Bar landslide" in 2018 (DFO 2020; DFO 2022):

<ul>
<li>Chinook: CK-10, MIDDLE FRASER RIVER_SP_1.3</li>
<li>Chinook: CK-11, MIDDLE FRASER RIVER_SU_1.3</li>
<li>Chinook: CK-12, UPPER FRASER RIVER_SP_1.3</li>
<li>Sockeye: SEL-06-14, TAKLA/TREMBLEUR-EARLY STUART TIMING</li>
</ul>

"Geological events" is not a large category to be assigned to appropriate legislation (Figure X). Aside from landscape-scale changes due to actions like forestry or mining, much of the nature of this category might not be viewed human-caused or managed. Subsequently, this threat has a small proportion of keywords that match the relevant legislation:

```{r geological-events-keywords-tags, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)

# 📁 Connect to the database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # 🔍 Extract matched keywords from paragraph_label_table
  geo_keywords <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT DISTINCT keyword
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'IUCN' AND label_value = '10.1 Geological Events'
  "))
  
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🎨 Render as styled tags
  if (nrow(geo_keywords) > 0) {
    cat("<div style='display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; margin-top: 10px;'>\n")
    for (kw in geo_keywords$keyword) {
      cat(sprintf("<span style='background-color: #f0f0f0; border-radius: 12px; padding: 6px 12px; font-size: 14px; font-family: sans-serif; border: 1px solid #ccc;'>%s</span>\n", kw))
    }
    cat("</div>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No matched keywords found for IUCN 10.1 Geological Events.</p>\n")
  }
}
```

The above keywords matched to the following amount of legislation:

```{r iucn-geological-events-tally, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)

db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # ✅ Step 1: Get IUCN-labeled paragraphs for Geological Events
  iucn_labels <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, label_value AS iucn_l2
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'IUCN' AND label_value = '10.1 Geological Events'
  "))
  
  # 📄 Step 2: Load paragraph metadata
  paragraph_meta <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, Section, legislation_id
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
    WHERE Section IS NOT NULL
  "))
  
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🔗 Step 3: Merge with metadata
  merged <- merge(iucn_labels, paragraph_meta, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  
  # 📊 Step 4: Tally by IUCN label
  iucn_tally <- merged[, .(
    clauses = uniqueN(paragraph_id),
    sections = uniqueN(paste(legislation_id, Section, sep = "_")),
    statutes = uniqueN(legislation_id)
  ), by = iucn_l2][order(iucn_l2)]
  
  # 🖥️ Output
  if (nrow(iucn_tally) > 0) {
    cat("<ul style='list-style-type: none; padding-left: 0; margin: 0;'>\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(iucn_tally))) {
      cat(sprintf("<li><strong>%s:</strong> %d statutes | %d sections | %d clauses</li>\n",
                  iucn_tally$iucn_l2[i],
                  iucn_tally$statutes[i],
                  iucn_tally$sections[i],
                  iucn_tally$clauses[i]
                  ))
    }
    cat("</ul>\n")
  } else {
    cat("<p>No IUCN labels found for Geological Events.</p>\n")
  }
}

```

```{r section-count-by-geological-events, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis', fig.width=12, fig.height=9}
# 📦 Load required libraries
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)

# 📁 Define path to the SQLite database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {
  # 🔌 Connect to the database
  conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = db_path)
  
  # 🗂️ Load paragraph labels filtered for Geological Events
  paragraph_labels <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id
    FROM paragraph_label_table
    WHERE label_type = 'IUCN' AND label_value = '10.1 Geological Events'
  "))
  
  # 🗂️ Load paragraph and legislation metadata including Section and legislation_name
  paragraph_table <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT paragraph_id, legislation_id, Section
    FROM LegislationParagraphs
  "))
  
  legislation_metadata <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "
    SELECT legislation_id, legislation_name, jurisdiction
    FROM LegislationMetadata
  "))
  
  # 🔌 Disconnect from the database
  dbDisconnect(conn)
  
  # 🔗 Join labels with paragraph and legislation metadata
  geo_data <- merge(paragraph_labels, paragraph_table, by = "paragraph_id", all.x = TRUE)
  geo_data <- merge(geo_data, legislation_metadata, by = "legislation_id", all.x = TRUE)
  
  # 📊 Summarize counts by unique Section-legislation_id pairs
  geo_counts <- geo_data[!is.na(Section), .(
    section_count = uniqueN(paste(Section, legislation_id))
  ), by = .(legislation_name, jurisdiction)]
  
  # 🧮 Order legislation by total section count
  geo_order <- geo_counts[, .(total = sum(section_count)), by = legislation_name][order(-total)]
  geo_counts[, legislation_name := factor(legislation_name, levels = rev(geo_order$legislation_name))]  # reverse for top-down
  
  # 🎨 Create horizontal bar chart
  ggplot(geo_counts, aes(
    x = section_count,
    y = legislation_name,
    fill = jurisdiction
  )) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c("Federal" = "#996666", "Provincial" = "#668899", "Unknown" = "#999999"),
      guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "Section Count for 10.1 Geological Events (IUCN)",
      x = "Unique Section Count",
      y = "Legislation Name",
      fill = "Jurisdiction"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
    )
}
```

  <em>Figure X. Description.</em>
</p>

```{r clause-type-pie-geological-events, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis', fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

# 📁 Connect to the database
db_path <- file.path(here("output"), "legislation.db")
if (!file.exists(db_path)) {
  cat("<p style='color:red;'>❌ Database file not found at: ", db_path, "</p>")
} else {

  geo_paragraphs <- data.table(dbGetQuery(conn, "

    WHERE label_type = 'IUCN' AND label_value = '10.1 Geological Events'

  "))

 # Choose a palette (e.g., "Royal1")

  labs(

}
```

## Appendix V - Case Study: IUCN 7.2 Dams & Water Management / Use

One IUCN threat was assessed as "Extreme-High" through COSEWIC Recovery Potential Assessment processes, which was "7.2 Dams & Water Management / Use" (DFO 2020). Water extraction, including groundwater, for irrigation and domestic purposes is listed as the most significant concern (DFO 2020). This threat was assigned to one Chinook conservation unit in the Fraser Interior area: 

<ul>
<li>Chinook: CK-16, SOUTH THOMPSON-BESSETTE CREEK_SU_1.2</li>
</ul>

"Dams and Water Management / Use" is one of the largest categories assigned to appropriate legislation (Figure X). Aside from pollution and fisheries, watercourse alterations are recognized as one of the top human activities that require regulation. Subsequently, this threat has a large proportion of keywords that match the relevant legislation:
